title: Prompt-Based Crime Scene Generation Using a Pre-Trained Diffusion Model
content: In forensic investigations crime scene visualization plays an important and core task. It has also been used extensively in criminal justice education, and law-enforcement training. However, obtaining diverse and realistic crime scene imagery is often challenging due to privacy concerns, legal restrictions, and the limited availability of publicly accessible datasets. Diffusion based generative models have significantly advanced recently and show power and remarkable capabilities in synthesizing realistic images from natural language descriptions. Although the model has been explored for creative content generation, virtual scene synthesis, domain-specific image production and text-to-image frameworks for generating contextual visual content across healthcare, education, and simulation environments. However, the application of diffusion models to crime scene generation remains relatively underexplored. In this research we investigate the feasibility of prompt-based crime scene generation using a pre-trained Stable Diffusion model. Four representative crime scene categories, namely burglary, accident, vandalism, and arson, were defined through carefully designed textual prompts. The diffusion model generated multiple synthetic crime scene images for each category. To assess semantic consistency between prompts and generated images we used CLIP-based similarity analysis. Quantitative evaluation revealed average CLIP similarity scores of 0.307 for arson scenes, 0.305 for accident scenes, 0.278 for vandalism scenes, and 0.247 for burglary scenes, indicating moderate to strong prompt-image alignment. The primary contribution of this work is the demonstration of a simple and reproducible framework for synthetic crime scene generation and evaluation using a pre-trained diffusion model. Future work will investigate larger prompt sets, automated forensic object detection, and human-centered evaluation of generated crime scene realism.
